references.text: The following verse in [ref:Luk 17:10|Luke 17:10] gives the direct conclusion to the question in verse 9: The servant deserves no thanks because he has only done his duty. The question in verse 9 is rhetorical and expects the answer "no".

In [ref:Matt 25:21-23|Matthew 25:21-23], the servants are praised for their faithfulness, but this concerns grace from the master, not that the servants have a claim to thanks – which highlights the tension with the rhetorical question in Luke 17:9 about whether a master owes his servant gratitude.

Paul asks in [ref:Rom 11:35|Romans 11:35]: "Who has given him anything first, so that he should receive repayment?" The thought is the same as in Luke 17:9: No one can demand anything from God for having done what was commanded.

In [ref:1 Kor 9:16-17|1 Corinthians 9:16-17], Paul says there is nothing to boast about in that he preaches the gospel, because it is a duty imposed on him. This reflects the principle in Luke 17:9 that the servant deserves no special thanks for doing what he was ordered.

In [ref:Filem 1:2-3|Philemon verses 2-3] (context for the whole letter), Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus in love – not out of duty. The entire letter to Philemon touches on the theme of duty versus grace, which is relevant to the question in Luke 17:9.

In [ref:Job 22:2-3|Job 22:2-3], Eliphaz asks: "Can a man be of benefit to God? ... Is it any gain to the Almighty that you are righteous?" The thought is related: human service creates no obligation on God, just as the master in Luke 17:9 does not owe the servant thanks.

In [ref:Luk 12:37|Luke 12:37], Jesus reverses the image: the master girds himself and serves his servants at the table. This shows the contrast to Luke 17:9 – God's grace goes far beyond what anyone can demand, even though the servant has no right to expect it.

In [ref:Joh 13:14-16|John 13:14-16], Jesus washes the disciples' feet and says that a servant is not greater than his master. The servant does what he was ordered, and cannot demand anything in return – the same principle as in Luke 17:9.
